title: The Accusative, Transitive Verbs, and Negation
summary: Transitive verbs take a direct object in the accusative; nouns, adjectives and pronouns all mark that case. The present tense of the first conjugation is given, and the rule that negation drives the object into the genitive is stated for recognition.

rules.heading: Transitive Verbs and the Direct Object
rules.statement: A **transitive verb** expresses an action that passes over from the subject to some other person or thing — one *sees* a house, *reads* a book. That other person or thing is the **direct object**, and in Lithuanian it is put into the **accusative case**. An intransitive verb, expressing an action confined to the subject, takes no object: *Berniukas dirba*, the boy works.

rules.heading: The Accusative Singular of Nouns
rules.statement: The accusative singular is formed by **shortening the ending to its bare vowel and adding the nosinė hook**. Each nominative ending has one accusative counterpart, and the correspondence admits no exceptions in the singular. Observe that masculine **-is** and **-ys** fall together in **-į**, so that the accusative alone will not tell you which the noun was.

paradigms.caption: Nominative → accusative singular
paradigms.footnote: Every accusative singular ending is a nosinė vowel. This is the grammatical work the hook does, and the reason it may never be omitted (see ¶3).

rules.heading: The Accusative of Adjectives
rules.statement: An adjective modifying a noun in the accusative is itself put into the accusative, agreeing as always in gender (¶17). The class in **-us / -i** is the only one that needs care: the feminine *graži* makes *gražią*, with an -i- that is not present in the masculine *gražų*.

examples.gloss: She is reading a new book.

rules.heading: The Accusative of the Personal Pronouns
rules.statement: The personal pronouns have their own accusative forms, which must be learned as a list. Unlike the nouns, they do not end in a nosinė vowel.

rules.heading: The Three Conjugations
rules.statement: Lithuanian verbs fall into **three conjugations**, distinguished by the ending of the **third person present**: **-a** (first), **-i** (second), **-o** (third). Since this form cannot be predicted from the infinitive, dictionaries cite every verb by three **principal parts** — infinitive, third person present, third person past — and this course does likewise. Learn the three parts together; from them every other form can be built.

paradigms.caption: The three conjugations, third person present
paradigms.footnote: The infinitive ending -ti is common to all three and says nothing about the conjugation.

examples.note: the form in which a verb is memorised

rules.heading: The Present Tense of the First Conjugation
rules.statement: The personal endings are added to the present stem, which is got by removing the **-a** of the third person present. As with *būti* (¶15), **one form serves the whole third person**, singular and plural, masculine and feminine alike. Because the ending already names the person, the subject pronoun is usually left out.

examples.note: Lithuanian has one present tense where English has two

footnotes: The present tense renders both the English simple present and the present progressive. *Jis rašo laišką* is equally "he writes a letter" and "he is writing a letter".

rules.heading: Negation of the Verb
rules.statement: A verb is negated by prefixing **ne-** and writing it as one word with the verb. The prefix draws the stress to itself in many words, but the spelling never separates it. The same *ne* standing alone is the word for "no".
footnotes: būti is irregular here: the third person negative is nėra, not *neyra (see ¶15).

rules.heading: The Object of a Negated Verb
rules.statement: When a transitive verb is negated, its direct object leaves the accusative and takes the **genitive** instead. The reason is that a negated verb asserts that no part of the thing was affected, and the genitive is the case of the part rather than the whole. The genitive is treated fully in the next section; for the present, **recognise** the change and do not be surprised by it.

examples.gloss: I do not see a house.

examples.target: Ji turi knygą. → Ji neturi knygos.
examples.gloss: She has a book. → She has no book.

rules.heading: The Conjunction Ir
rules.statement: **Ir** joins words or clauses of like kind, as English *and*. Joined objects each stand in the accusative, the case being repeated and not merely understood.

examples.target: Ji valgo obuolį ir geria arbatą.
examples.gloss: She eats an apple and drinks tea.
I see a house and a cat.

drills.stem: What is the accusative singular of **knyga**?
drills.explanation: Feminine -a makes -ą. *knygos* is the genitive, which appears after a negated verb (¶26).

drills.stem: How many cases does the Lithuanian noun have?
drills.explanation: Seven. Two of them — the nominative and the accusative — have now been met.
*skaitau* is the first person, and the object takes the accusative *knygą*. Note that one Lithuanian present serves for both "I read" and "I am reading".
First-conjugation endings are -u, -i, -a, -ame, -ate, -a. *dirbate* belongs to jūs.

drills.stem: Which of these are correct **accusative singular** forms?
drills.explanation: namas → namą, katė → katę, sūnus → sūnų. *brolis* is still the nominative; the accusative is *brolį*.
Both the adjective and the noun go into the accusative, and the adjective agrees in gender: *didelis* → *didelį* beside *namas* → *namą*.
The third needs the accusative pronoun *tave*, the fourth the accusative *laišką*. In the first, feminine *graži* makes *gražią*.

drills.stem: *Aš matau namą* becomes, in the negative:
drills.explanation: Two things change together: *ne-* is written onto the verb as one word, and the object leaves the accusative for the genitive *namo*.

drills.stem: Which statements about the third person of a Lithuanian verb are correct?
options: One form serves both the singular and the plural.
It has separate masculine and feminine forms.
Its ending tells you which conjugation the verb belongs to.
It is the second of the three principal parts a dictionary gives.
drills.explanation: *jis dirba* and *jie dirba* are alike, and gender makes no difference to the verb. The ending of that form — -a, -i or -o — names the conjugation, which is why dictionaries cite it.

drills.title: Petras ir Rūta
drills.passage: Jonas yra mokytojas. Jis turi brolį. Brolis yra Petras. Petras skaito naują knygą. Jonas rašo laišką. Rūta valgo obuolį ir geria arbatą. Ji nemato brolio.
drills.translation: Jonas is a teacher. He has a brother. The brother is Petras. Petras is reading a new book. Jonas is writing a letter. Rūta is eating an apple and drinking tea. She does not see the brother.

questions.explanation: *Petras skaito naują knygą* — adjective and noun both accusative. The letter is Jonas's.

questions.stem: Which statements does the passage support?
questions.explanation: Petras reads; it is Jonas who writes. The other three are stated word for word.

questions.stem: How many **direct objects in the accusative** appear in the passage?
questions.explanation: brolį, knygą, laišką, obuolį, arbatą — five. *brolio* in the last sentence is a genitive, because *nemato* is negated (¶26), and so does not count.
